Several trait states showed higher than average correlation ratios with these clusters, indicating strong contributions to species separation into functional groups (shown in bold in Table 2). Species in clusters 1 and 2 were characterized by high ecological specialization. Species in cluster 1 were primarily characterized by specialization to few and locally distributed host plants, but did not show a strong habitat specialization as they were associated with several different types of open habitats (e.g. grassland, heath). In contrast, species in cluster 2 were characterized by strong habitat specialization, especially to forest habitat, but were less restricted in their host plant use. Both groups were characterized by low mobility (i.e. non-migratory) and overwintering in immature stages (egg, larvae). Unlike these two specialist groups, species in cluster 3 had mature overwintering stages (adult, pupa), were highly mobile (i.e. migratory) and showed no particular host plant- or habitat specialization. The three clusters are subsequently referred to as ‘sedentary host plant specialists (cluster 1), ‘sedentary habitat specialists’ (cluster 2) and ‘mobile generalists’ (cluster 3). Although simplistic, these names are meant to highlight some of the key ecological traits of each functional group.

[prose] Sedentary habitat specialist species were often associated with forest habitats (Tables 2 and S6), including the Northern Chequered Skipper (Carterocephalus silvicola), Clouded Apollo (Parnassius mnemosyne) and Purple Emperor (Apatura ilia). Although several species within this group were associated with semi-natural grassland, including some species of high conservation concern, for example silver-spotted skipper (Hesperia comma), population trajectories for this group are likely to have been strongly influenced by historical forest management practices. During the 20th century, deciduous woodlands of lowland temperate Europe have become increasingly dense and shady due to the replacement of millennia-old management techniques by even-aged tall forest stands, with deleterious impacts for butterflies (Warren & Key, 1991; Bergman & Kindvall, 2004; Spitzer et al., 2008). Furthermore, species-rich ecotones marking the transition zone between closed and open vegetation, and which often harbour high species diversity, including many forest butterflies, have increasingly been replaced by sharp borders. This has had detrimental effects on butterflies such as Ilex Hairstreak (Satyrium ilicis) (Maes et al., 2014). [prose] Results We document severe declines in butterfly diversity over the last century, with substantial regional-scale extinctions leading to a net loss of 10% of all Danish butterfly species. Segregating species into functional groups showed that the highest rate of regional extinction occurred among sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage, while the most severe local-scale declines occurred among sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage. In contrast, mobile generalist species with mature overwintering stages showed stable richness trends throughout the century. However, a pervasive spatio-temporal biotic homogenization of butterfly assemblages was revealed for all functional groups.

[prose] Figure 1 Species richness changes (estimated weighted mean  95% confidence intervals) for (a) all Danish butterfly species, (b) cluster 1 (sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage) (c) cluster 2 (sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage) and (d) cluster 3 (mobile generalists with mature overwintering stages). The three functional groups (b–c) correspond to clusters 1–3 in Table 2, which were obtained using hierarchical clustering and species-specific values of eight ecological traits (Table 1). Observed distribution records were initially binned into six time slices (1900–19, 1920–39, 1940–59, 1960–79, 1980–99 and 2000–12) and richness changes were then estimated for each time slice relative to the most recent time slice (i.e. 2000–12). The most recent time slice serves as a baseline for comparison among time slices with its value being set at 100. Richness changes are shown for two different spatial resolutions (10 km9 10 km and all of Denmark).

[prose] Our analysis showed that butterfly species could be segregated into three clearly separated functional groups, which showed marked differences in the strength, timing and spatial scale of richness change. The highest rate of regional extinction occurred among sedentary habitat specialists overwintering in the egg stage (cluster 2), while the most severe local-scale losses occurred among sedentary host plant specialists overwintering in the larval stage (cluster 1). In contrast, mobile species with broad ecological adaptations and mature overwintering stages (cluster 3) were stable throughout the century.

[prose] Eight species trait categories, which have been suggested to be important for butterfly responses to global change (Henle et al., 2004; Poyry € et al., 2009; Ockinger € et al., 2010; Diamond et al., 2011), were included in the analysis. These traits were extracted from the literature on Danish butterflies (Stoltze, 1996; Garcıa-Barros, 2000; Frederiksen et al., 2006) and represented overwintering stage, migratory behaviour, degree of habitat openness, habitat specialization, larval host plant distribution, voltinity (number of generations per year), body size and host plant specialization (larval dietary breadth). We defined trait categories using local knowledge, that is ‘realized’ niches. Even if a species can be considered a generalist on the European scale, but a specialist in Denmark (due to missing alternatives or different ecological conditions), it is the loss of these particular resources (i.e. habitat types or food plants) which makes a species decline in Denmark, regardless of the potential at larger scales.
